lead: Clustering has no target label by default, so you cannot score it like a classifier. Evaluation asks two questions: are points inside a cluster close, and are different clusters far apart? Internal measures answer this using distances only. External measures compare clusters with known true labels. These scores guide the choice of k, distance and algorithm in market segmentation, image grouping and document sorting. Advanced: only a few universities teach this.
prereq: You need: K-means and hierarchical clustering, plus Euclidean distance from Unit 1.

blocks.text: Cohesion measures how tight a cluster is. Separation measures how far clusters lie from each other. For a point i, let a(i) be the mean distance from i to the other points in its own cluster. Let b(i) be the smallest mean distance from i to all points in any other cluster. Small a is good; large b is good.

blocks.where: s(i) is the silhouette of point i; a(i) is the mean distance to its own cluster; b(i) is the smallest mean distance to another cluster. The value lies in [−1, 1]. Near 1: point is closer to its own cluster. Near 0: point is on a boundary. Negative: point may be in the wrong cluster. The cluster silhouette is the mean of s(i).

blocks.text: Davies–Bouldin (DB) averages, over clusters, the worst ratio of within-cluster spread to between-cluster separation. Lower DB is better. Calinski–Harabasz (CH) is between-cluster dispersion divided by within-cluster dispersion, scaled by (n−k)/(k−1); higher CH is better. Here n is the number of points and k is the number of clusters.

sections.h3: External measures: labels as ground truth

blocks.text: External measures need a true class for each point. Purity gives each cluster the label of its majority class, then counts correct points divided by n. It rises easily when k is large, so it is a rough check.

The Rand index compares every pair of points. A pair is an agreement if both cluster and truth put the pair together, or both keep it apart. RI = agreements / all pairs, in [0, 1]. Adjusted Rand index (ARI) subtracts the agreement expected by chance; 0 means random, 1 is perfect. Normalised mutual information (NMI) compares the cluster partition with the label partition; 0 to 1, higher is better.

Use internal measures when labels are absent. Use external measures only when true labels exist and are trusted. Neither score alone proves a clustering is meaningful; check stability and the business use.

figure.caption: A and B sit one unit apart in one cluster; C is 5.6569 from A in another cluster. The two distances feed A's silhouette: a = 1, b = 5.6569.

spec.aria: Points A(0,0) and B(0,1) are in cluster one, one unit apart; point C(4,4) is in cluster two, 5.6569 units from A.

examples.question: Points A(0,0) and B(0,1) are in cluster 1; C(4,4) is in cluster 2. Using Euclidean distance, compute the silhouette score of A. Use a = mean distance to other points in its own cluster and b = smallest mean distance to another cluster.
steps: Own cluster of A is {A, B}. The only other point is B. a = distance(A,B) = √((0−0)²+(1−0)²) = 1.
The other cluster is {C}. Mean distance from A to {C} is distance(A,C) = √((4−0)²+(4−0)²) = √32 = 5.6569. Since there is one other cluster, b = 5.6569.
examples.answer: The silhouette score of A is 0.8232; A is much closer to its own cluster than to the other cluster.
examples.check:
import math
a = 1.0
b = math.sqrt(32)
s = (b - a) / max(a, b)
print(f"{a:.4f}")
print(f"{b:.4f}")
print(f"{s:.4f}")

traps: Do not use purity or ARI when you have no true labels; they need ground truth.
Silhouette is bounded by −1 and 1, not 0 and 1; a negative value is a warning, not a calculation error.
Davies–Bouldin is lower-is-better; Calinski–Harabasz and silhouette are higher-is-better.
Silhouette needs a distance. Changing the distance changes a(i), b(i) and the score.
High purity can come from many small clusters; compare at the same k and with ARI.

quiz.q: Define cohesion and separation in one line each.
quiz.a: Cohesion: how close points inside a cluster are. Separation: how far different clusters are from each other.

quiz.q: Why can't purity be used when true labels are absent?
quiz.a: Purity assigns each cluster the majority true class and counts correct points; without true classes there is no majority label to compare with.

quiz.q: For B(0,1), own cluster {A,B}, other cluster {C}, compute the silhouette score of B using Euclidean distance.
RI = 0.9 and ARI = 0.05 for one clustering. What does this suggest?
quiz.a: Many pairs agree by chance because most pairs are apart. After chance correction, agreement is near random, so the clustering is not aligned with the labels.

quiz.q: Two runs give Davies–Bouldin scores 0.8 and 1.5. Which run is better on this measure?
quiz.a: The run with 0.8 is better, because lower Davies–Bouldin is better.

quiz.q: Why can a point's silhouette be negative in overlapping clusters?
quiz.a: Its mean distance to its own cluster a is larger than its smallest mean distance to another cluster b, so b−a is negative and the point looks misplaced.

beyond: Not for the exam. Practitioners check cluster stability by re-running on bootstrap samples and measuring how often pairs stay together. The gap statistic compares within-cluster dispersion with that of a null reference. Consensus clustering combines many runs. Search for silhouette analysis, bootstrap stability, gap statistic and adjusted Rand index.
